title: How the independent rear suspension works
introduction:
The rear suspension has three connected jobs: support the car, guide each wheel and control its movement. Springs carry the load, the arms and links locate the wheel, and the shock absorber keeps the movement controlled. Understanding those roles makes the component list much more useful than a collection of names.

Open the [rear suspension component map](#/document/G1697533) to match the names below to their locations.

edits.text: These components work together in the rear suspension:

edits.why: Support the load and allow the suspension to compress and extend.
Provide the lower locating connection while allowing controlled movement at the mounting points.
Control suspension movement in partnership with the springs.
Help resist body lean and sway.
Help establish the direction each rear wheel points.
Provide the upper locating connection to each wheel knuckle.
Connect the associated rear suspension parts as shown in the component-location drawing.

edits.text: Wheel bearing and wheel hub assemblies
edits.why: Support the rotating wheel at the knuckle.
Connect the wheel-end assembly to the suspension links.
Provide the threaded attachment points for the wheels.

edits.text:
Each rear side uses 2 parallel arms: 1 upper and 1 lower. Each arm attaches to the chassis at one end and to the wheel knuckle at the other. This arrangement lets the rear wheels respond to road imperfections independently.

The shock absorber attaches to the lower arm and works with the spring to control up-and-down movement. The stabilizer bar and its links control lean and sway.
edits.why: Independent wheel movement and controlled body roll are compatible: the arms guide each wheel, while the bar helps coordinate the sides under roll.
